B04_00: Aerobic metabolism generates superoxide and hydrogen peroxide, and a set of enzymes converts these oxidants to water and oxygen before they damage lipids, proteins and DNA, while also setting the strength and duration of peroxide signalling. Compartment-specific superoxide dismutases pass hydrogen peroxide to catalase, glutathione peroxidases and peroxiredoxins, which NADPH-dependent thioredoxin and glutathione reductase systems regenerate. NADPH oxidases and ER oxidoreductases generate peroxide, and copper chaperones load dismutases with metal.
B04_01: Heme oxygenase 1 cleaves heme into biliverdin, carbon monoxide and free iron, removing a pro-oxidant cofactor as part of a cytoprotective stress response. At antioxidant response elements, small MAF proteins pair either with NFE2L2 to activate its gene or with the heme-sensing repressor BACH1 to silence it, so rising heme relieves repression. The enzyme acts as an ER-anchored dimer until intramembrane proteolysis releases a soluble form.
B04_02: Reactive oxygen species can drive a cell into irreversible proliferative arrest. Oxidised thioredoxin releases the kinase ASK1 (MAP3K5), activating p38 and JNK cascades; p38-activated MAPKAPK kinases phosphorylate BMI1 and p53, while JNK-driven AP-1 induces the H3K27me3 demethylase KDM6B. Both routes evict Polycomb repressors from the CDKN2A locus, raising p16INK4A to block CDK4/6-mediated RB inactivation and p14ARF to stabilise p53 against MDM2.
B04_03: Under oxidative stress the transcription factor NRF2, partnered with a small MAF protein at antioxidant response elements and recruiting the acetyltransferase coactivators CREBBP and EP300, induces pentose phosphate pathway enzymes: glucose-6-phosphate and 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenases plus transketolase and transaldolase. This diverts glucose from glycolysis toward NADPH, which regenerates reduced glutathione and thioredoxin, and toward ribose-5-phosphate for nucleotide synthesis, coupling redox sensing to central carbon metabolism.
B04_04: Proteotoxic stress triggers a transcriptional programme that increases chaperone production, and switching it on and off is controlled at the level of HSF1. HSP70 chaperones with DNAJ and BAG co-chaperones hold HSF1 monomeric until unfolded substrates compete them away; HSF1 then trimerises, enters the nucleus with the carrier HIKESHI and binds DNA. Phosphorylation by GSK3B and ERK-MAPKAPK2, SIRT1 deacetylation and ubiquitin-mediated turnover tune the amplitude and duration of the response.
B04_05: Accumulation of unfolded proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum activates IRE1, which splices XBP1 mRNA to produce an active transcription factor that expands ER folding and processing capacity as an adaptive, pro-survival output. Spliced XBP1 binds ER stress response elements together with NF-Y, inducing chaperones and co-chaperones, protein disulfide isomerases, ER-associated degradation components, and translocon and trafficking factors. Without this output, persistent ER stress tips cells toward apoptosis.
B04_06: Cells that have permanently exited the cell cycle secrete a programme of cytokines, chemokines and growth-factor binding proteins that reinforces their arrest and signals to neighbouring cells. DNA damage raises CDKN1A, restraining CDK2 so that APC/C-FZR1 degrades the methyltransferases EHMT1 and EHMT2, de-repressing IL6 and CXCL8 promoters. RAS-MAPK-activated CEBPB cooperates with NF-kappa-B there, IL6-STAT3 and IL1A feedback sustain output, and AP-1 drives IL1A and IGFBP7.
B04_07: The heat shock response is actively terminated once chaperone capacity again matches the unfolded-protein load. Newly made HSP70 and DNAJB1, freed from unfolded substrates, bind and silence HSF1 trimers; HSP90 complexes with FKBP4 and PTGES3 favour the inactive state; HSBP1 blocks DNA binding and transactivation; and p300/CBP acetylation lowers HSF1 occupancy at heat shock elements. The trimers then leave promoters and revert to inactive monomers.
B04_08: Accumulation of misfolded proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum triggers cleavage of membrane-bound ATF6-alpha, releasing its cytosolic bZIP fragment to the nucleus to induce genes that restore folding capacity. The fragment recognises the CCACG motif of ER stress response elements together with the trimeric CCAAT-binding factor NF-Y, driving chaperones such as BiP, GRP94 and calreticulin plus XBP1, ATF4 and CHOP, linking adaptive folding capacity to survival or apoptosis decisions.
B04_09: Strong mitogenic signalling, such as hyperactive RAS/RAF/ERK output or unrestrained E2F activity, can trigger permanent withdrawal from the cell cycle. Arrest converges on the CDKN2A locus: p16INK4A inhibits CDK4 and CDK6 so RB stays hypophosphorylated and E2F targets silent, while p14ARF inhibits MDM2 to stabilise p53. ERK-phosphorylated ETS1 and ETS2 drive p16INK4A transcription against ID1, p15INK4B contributes, and microRNA-24 with Argonaute limits translation of both transcripts.
B04_10: Transcription of the NFE2L2 gene, encoding the antioxidant master regulator NRF2, is controlled separately from NRF2 protein stability and sets the ceiling on cellular stress defences. MYC, the NF-kappaB p65/p50 dimer and the NOTCH1 intracellular domain act at its promoter, NRF2 with a small MAF partner autoregulates its own gene, and CREBBP and EP300 provide acetyltransferase coactivation, coupling proliferative, inflammatory and developmental signals to antioxidant capacity.
B04_11: Beyond inducing antioxidant genes, the transcription factor NFE2L2 reprograms central carbon metabolism by driving expression of IDH1 and ME1, NADPH-generating dehydrogenases acting on isocitrate and malate. This couples the response to oxidative and electrophilic stress with the supply of reducing equivalents for regenerating glutathione and thioredoxin and of carbon skeletons for lipid and nucleotide synthesis, linking redox homeostasis to anabolic metabolism.
B04_12: Membrane-anchored bZIP transcription factors of the CREB3/OASIS family couple secretory pathway load to gene expression. Each sits in the ER membrane with its DNA-binding and activation domains facing the cytosol; in the Golgi it is cleaved sequentially by MBTPS1 and MBTPS2, freeing a fragment that enters the nucleus to activate genes expanding secretory capacity, opposed by CREBRF. Unlike ATF6, they do not sense unfolded protein via BiP release.
B04_13: Besides antioxidant genes, the transcription factor NFE2L2 tunes inflammatory gene expression, linking cellular redox state to immune signalling. Bound with a small MAF partner at antioxidant response elements, it recruits the acetyltransferases CREBBP and EP300 to remodel chromatin at chemokine promoters such as CCL2. Its effect is context-dependent: it can activate such genes directly while indirectly restraining NF-kB-driven inflammatory transcription, partly through induction of heme oxygenase-1.
B04_14: Accumulation of misfolded ER proteins leads, via PERK-mediated eIF2alpha phosphorylation, to increased ATF4 translation and a transcriptional programme that either restores proteostasis or commits the cell to apoptosis. ATF4, combining with C/EBP partners and NF-Y, induces HERPUD1, asparagine synthetase, IGFBP1, inflammatory chemokines and CHOP, with ATF3 feedback and a parallel ATF6 branch. Cytoplasmic exosome, deadenylase and KHSRP-mediated mRNA decay set how long these stress transcripts persist.
B04_15: The transcription factor NRF2 controls how much xenobiotic a cell retains by inducing drug efflux transporters and multidrug-resistance enzymes. Bound with a small Maf protein such as MAFK at antioxidant response elements, it recruits CREBBP and EP300 to acetylate histones and open target promoters. Induced targets include the ATP-binding cassette pumps ABCC1 and ABCC3, which export glutathione and drug conjugates, the broad efflux pump ABCG2, and ABCF2.
B04_16: The degradation rate of the transcription factor NFE2L2 sets cellular capacity for oxidative and electrophilic stress responses, and besides KEAP1-CUL3 a second route uses an SCF ubiquitin ligase of CUL1, SKP1, RBX1 and the receptor BTRC. After priming phosphorylation, GSK3B phosphorylates a DSGIS motif in the Neh6 domain, creating a phosphodegron that BTRC recognises; polyubiquitination targets NFE2L2 to the 26S proteasome. Because AKT inhibits GSK3B, growth-factor signalling stabilises NFE2L2.
B04_17: In the unfolded protein response, the ER membrane transcription factor ATF6B is held through its lumenal domain by the chaperone BiP; misfolded protein accumulation releases BiP and exposes Golgi targeting signals. There the proteases MBTPS1 and MBTPS2 sequentially cleave it, freeing a bZIP fragment that enters the nucleus and induces chaperone and ER quality-control genes. As a weak activator heterodimerising with ATF6, it dampens rather than amplifies the response.
B04_18: The transcriptional repressor BACH1, partnered with small Maf proteins such as MAFK, occupies Maf recognition elements at antioxidant and heme-handling genes such as heme oxygenase-1, keeping them silent until heme or oxidants rise. BACH1 abundance is limited by an SCF ubiquitin ligase of SKP1, CUL1 and RBX1 with the receptors FBXL17 or SKP2, which targets it for proteasomal degradation, and by microRNAs such as miR-155 and let-7.
B04_19: Beyond antioxidant genes, the transcription factor NRF2 controls targets of the ER stress response, notably ATF4. Bound with a small MAF partner at antioxidant response elements and recruiting the acetyltransferase coactivators CREBBP and EP300, NRF2 induces ATF4, which activates adaptive metabolic and chaperone genes, including serine and glycine biosynthesis, under hypoxia, amino acid limitation or unfolded protein load, but promotes apoptosis under sustained stress, linking redox sensing to proteostasis.
B04_20: Proteotoxic stress activates HSF1, the switch for the heat shock response. Inactive HSF1 monomers are held by HSP90 and HSP70 chaperones; stress releases them, and HSF1 trimerises, accumulates in the nucleus and binds heat shock elements to induce chaperones and co-chaperones such as DNAJB1, HSPB1, HSPH1 and ubiquitin. Newly made chaperones and HSBP1 return HSF1 to monomers, while acetylation, RNA-binding inputs and RPA-mediated promoter access tune amplitude.
B04_21: When reactive oxygen species or electrophiles accumulate, NRF2 escapes degradation, enters the nucleus and binds antioxidant response elements with small MAF proteins, competing with the repressor BACH1 and recruiting CREBBP and EP300 coactivators. It induces glutathione synthesis and recycling, SLC7A11-mediated cystine import, glutathione transferase conjugation, NQO1 quinone reduction, HMOX1 heme catabolism and thioredoxin- and peroxiredoxin-based peroxide removal, with ATF4 linking it to integrated stress signalling.
B04_22: Permanent cell-cycle exit after irreparable DNA damage or telomere shortening is locked in by assembling heterochromatin foci: each chromosome condenses into a punctate focus of H3K9-methylated heterochromatin, and E2F-driven proliferation genes are silenced. The HIRA-ASF1A-UBN1-CABIN1 chaperone complex stages at PML bodies, then deposits histone H3.3 at forming foci, accompanied by HMGA proteins, linker histone changes and lamin B1 loss. Formation requires RB1 and TP53 signalling, with CDKN1A enforcing arrest.
B04_23: When constitutively stabilised, the transcription factor NRF2 drives a programme promoting cell survival and proliferation beyond its antioxidant role. As a heterodimer with small MAF proteins such as MAFK, recruiting the coactivators CREBBP and EP300 with SP1 aiding promoter occupancy, NRF2 induces the anti-apoptotic genes BCL2 and BCL2L1, mitogens such as AREG, EGF and PDGFA, and NOTCH1 signalling components, coupling cytoprotection to growth-factor autonomy and developmental signalling.
